A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InvFussion/InvFusion research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable matching despite renaming and reformatting.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendices B–C report original FFHQ and ImageNet restoration, generation, MMSE and neural posterior principal-component results.

after.justification: The original empirical evaluations remain, supplemented by architectural ablations, consistency measurements, Poisson-noise experiments and additional method comparisons.

M1.justification: The feature-degradation layer, joint-attention conditioning, diffusion and MMSE objectives, and NPPC procedure are retained. The new pseudocode documents implementation details without establishing an algorithm revision. Applying blocks selectively was already described in v1 Appendix A.1.

E1.justification: The datasets, resolutions and principal tasks remain unchanged. v2 Table 12 adds a high-Poisson-noise scenario for FFHQ64 motion blur and in-painting, extending the existing noiseless and Gaussian-noise coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MGPS and InDI to the FFHQ64, ImageNet64 and FFHQ256 comparisons; MGPS is spelled MPGS in Table 13. Tables 14–15 additionally compare against end-to-end unrolled DDRM and ASeq-DIP. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparator families. InDI was previously cited but not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds LPIPS and measurement-space MSE evaluations, controlled block-resolution configurations, ten-step DDRM unrolling trained with MSE, and a 1,024-image PSNR/KID/LPIPS comparison with ASeq-DIP. Table 6 also reports bf16 for FFHQ256, whereas v1 Appendix A.1 specified fp16 generally. These are new evaluation designs and a reported setting revision, without establishing which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained out-of-distribution, Gaussian-noise and MMSE-training analyses, v2 adds progressive block-placement ablations (Table 8), direct measurement-consistency diagnostics (Table 10), and a high-Poisson-noise failure test (Table 12). These examine architectural contribution and robustness limits not directly tested in v1. The dedicated MMSE-versus-Palette visual comparison in v1 Figure 4 is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions describe deterministic sampling with matched seeds for qualitative comparisons. Neither introduces repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The existing NPPC uncertainty-estimation application is retained.

E6.justification: Changes exceed rounding: FFHQ64 motion-blur CFID changes from 4.69 to 4.2 (Table 1), and FFHQ unconditional FID changes from 6.27 to 6.36 (Table 4). ImageNet in-painting CFID changes from 6.44 to 5.9, reversing the comparison with Palette's 6.20/6.2. Numerous new analysis and comparator results, plus FFHQ256 MMSE rows, substantially expand the findings. Updated FFHQ256 scores accompany a revised reported precision setting.

T1.justification: The diffusion formulation, posterior-mixture reasoning, feature-degradation equation, training objectives and high-noise MMSE argument are retained. Some definitions move inline and equations are renumbered, but no substantive mathematical definition, proof or derivation is added or revised.

C1.justification: v2 explicitly claims the first training-based degradation-aware posterior sampler in its abstract and introduction. It also replaces adaptation to 'virtually any degradation' with a 'wide range' and emphasizes comparisons among models handling multiple tasks. The central architectural, sampling, MMSE and NPPC contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the broad noise-generalization expectation with observed failure under high Poisson noise and explains limitations of comparing DIP methods with posterior samplers. It also discusses unseen matrix operators as generalization evidence and connects a prospective nonlinear extension to latent diffusion. Existing training-coverage, linearity and computational limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.2 supplies pseudocode for feature degradation and joint attention, including key construction. Appendix A.1 adds hardware, approximate training times, licenses and per-experiment precision information. Its planned code/checkpoint-release statement becomes a statement of code availability; v1 already contained a repository link, so the link itself is not a new resource disclosure.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for ASeq-DIP, MGPS, an algorithm-unrolling review, KID and LPIPS. It more explicitly distinguishes posterior sampling from distortion-oriented unrolling and DIP objectives, and strengthens its novelty positioning. Most of the existing related-work discussion and cited literature remain.

P1.justification: InvFussion is renamed InvFusion, the abstract is substantially rewritten, and introduction and explanatory passages receive localized revisions. The main section sequence remains intact. The appendix gains pseudocode and ablation sections, while Additional Results moves from Appendix C to D; most existing exposition is retained.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column NeurIPS format, with extensive relocation and resizing of displays. Six new tables and code listings are added, and existing comparison tables expand. v1 Figure 4 is removed; the NPPC figure is redrawn with explicit model-flow annotations, while the unconditional sample grids are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central architecture through previously missing block-placement controls and direct consistency measurements, while the Poisson experiment establishes a concrete failure boundary. Broader comparators and implementation pseudocode improve credibility and reproducibility. New reporting problems include incorrect LPIPS highlighting in Table 9 and unexplained MMSE differences between Tables 1 and 7, but these limited issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.
